t: An heir who is still a minor
p: Paul pictures a rich man's son who owns everything and yet has no say in his own life.
b: The picture is simple. A boy will inherit the whole estate, but while he is a minor (Greek nepios, a child under age) he is under epitropoi (guardians, who look after the child) and oikonomoi (managers, who look after the property). He is treated like a household slave until the day his father has named. Scholars argue about whose law Paul has in mind. Roman law set the ages by statute, so a father could not simply pick the date, while Greek and Egyptian practice varied (Burton lays out the evidence). Paul is probably not teaching law. He borrows a familiar scene to say that God's people lived for a time under supervision, and that the time has now ended. The same thought runs through 3:23-25 and 4:3. The Plain English Translation says 'minor' here and at 4:3, 'son' for huios (4:6-7), and keeps 'child' for teknon (4:19, 25, 27-31). Paul's contrast is between the nepios, who is like a slave, and the huios, who has the standing of an heir.

p: Paul's phrase stoicheia tou kosmou has at least five meanings that scholars defend.
b: Stoicheia means things lined up in a row: letters of the alphabet, then the basic parts of anything. The readings: (1) the four physical elements, earth, air, fire and water, which some people worshipped as gods (Wisdom of Solomon 13:2 names fire, wind, air, stars and water; Wisdom of Solomon 7:17 uses the word stoicheia); (2) the ABCs, the first lessons of religion, Jewish and pagan alike (the sense in Hebrews 5:12); (3) spirit beings who ruled the stars and the elements (Colossians 2:8; Testament of Solomon 8; Arnold argues for this); (4) the pairs of opposites on which the old world stood, such as Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female (some scholars read 3:28 and 6:15 beside it); (5) any basic rules that bind a people before Christ. The Plain English Translation keeps the literal word and lets the reader see how Paul uses it again at 4:9.
orig: στοιχεῖα τοῦ κόσμου (stoicheia tou kosmou), 'the elements of the world'
r: 4:9; Colossians 2:8; Colossians 2:20; Hebrews 5:12; Wisdom of Solomon 7:17; Wisdom of Solomon 13:2; Testament of Solomon 8:2

a: He was born of a woman.
p: Paul says the Son 'came to be' from a woman. What does that add, and what does it leave out?
b: Paul's verb is ginomai, 'to come to be', not gennao, 'to be fathered or to give birth'. (The Plain English Translation says 'born' for both verbs, here and at 4:23 and 4:29, so the difference does not show in English.) Some readers have found a hint of the virgin birth in the choice. Most scholars reject that: Paul uses ginomai of ordinary births too (Romans 1:3), and in this chapter he uses gennao for Ishmael and Isaac (4:23, 29). 'Born of woman' is also a Hebrew way to say 'a mortal human being' (Job 14:1; Job 15:14). The plain point is that the Son shared human life, and that the sending of the Son (4:4) is matched by the sending of the Spirit (4:6). Paul never mentions Mary, Joseph or Bethlehem. The churches read that silence differently; see the card on this verse.
orig: γενόμενον ἐκ γυναικός (genomenon ek gynaikos), 'coming to be from a woman'

a: He was born under the law.
t: Jesus, a Jew under the law
p: One of the clearest places where Paul says Jesus lived as a Jew under the Torah.
b: 'Under the law' (hypo nomon) means placed under the Law of Moses. Paul says Jesus himself was born into that position. Luke tells of his circumcision on the eighth day and the offering at the Temple (Luke 2:21-24). Jewish readers of Paul stress that Paul never imagines Jesus as someone who stepped outside Judaism. Who, then, are 'those under the law' in 4:5? Views: Jews only, among them Jewish believers; Jews and Gentiles alike, since all lived under the 'elements' in one form or another; Paul's 'we' in 4:3 shifts between the two groups. The Plain English Translation leaves the pronouns as the Greek has them. See also 3:23-25 and the note at 4:3.

p: Paul takes a family word from the Roman world and makes it a promise about God.
b: The Greek is huiothesia, 'placing as a son'. In the Roman world an adopted son took on the family name and the right to inherit, and an adopted adult could be chosen because the family wanted him. Israel had no adoption law of this kind; Paul uses the Greek custom to show how Gentile believers enter God's family. In Romans the same word is used of Israel (Romans 9:4) and of believers: "You received the Spirit of adoption as children. By that Spirit we call out, "Abba, Father!"" (Romans 8:15). Galatians 4:5-7 and Romans 8:14-17 say nearly the same thing, and the Spirit is the proof in both. The Plain English Translation keeps 'sons' for the Greek huioi; see the note at 4:6.

p: Paul writes 'sons' because sons inherited, and he means women and men alike.
b: The Greek is huioi, 'sons'. Paul uses three different words in this part of the letter: nepios, a minor under age, who is no better off than a slave (4:1, 3); huios, a son with the standing of an heir (4:6-7); and teknon, 'child', for the family tie (4:19, 25, 27-31). The Plain English Translation keeps the three apart so that Paul's contrast stays visible in English: a minor is like a slave, a son is an heir. In the law and custom Paul's readers knew, it was sons who were the heirs, so the word carries the inheritance. Paul has just said that in Christ there is 'no male and female' (3:28), and he now gives all believers, women and men, the status of sons and heirs. He does not mean that believers are male; he means that every believer has the standing the heir had in the household. The Plain English Translation keeps 'sons' for this reason, and to match 3:26. The KJV also keeps 'sons'. Other books of this Plain English Translation may render huioi as 'children' where no such contrast is at work (compare Romans 8:14-16).

p: An Aramaic word for father, said by Jesus, now shouted in Greek by Gentile believers.
b: Abba is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jesus. Mark remembers the prayer in Gethsemane this way: "Abba, Father," he was saying, "for you anything is possible." (Mark 14:36). The Galatians spoke Greek, yet Paul says the Spirit cries out in the very word Jesus used, and Romans 8:15 says the same. That shows how early the word had become part of Christian prayer, in Greek-speaking churches far from Jerusalem. A popular claim says abba means 'Daddy'. James Barr argued in 1988 that this goes too far: the word was used by adult children too, and it means 'my father' or 'Father'. The new thing is not baby talk but the access. Slaves could not call the master Father; children could. Notice also who cries: here the Spirit; in Romans 8:15, 'we' do.
orig: ἀββά ὁ πατήρ (abba ho pater), 'Abba, the Father'

t: What the Galatians used to worship
p: Before they heard the good news the Galatians served gods that are 'no gods', as Israel's prophets said.
b: Paul addresses Gentiles who once served the gods of Anatolia and Greece. The region had the great temple of the Mother of the Gods at Pessinus (Strabo, Geography 12.5.3), local gods of the hills, and the worship of the emperor. Acts shows how a crowd at Lystra reacted to a healing by calling Barnabas and Paul Zeus and Hermes (Acts 14:11-13). 'No gods' is the language of Israel's Scriptures about idols (Deuteronomy 32:21; Jeremiah 2:11; Isaiah 37:19), and it was how Jewish teachers described the nations' gods (compare 1 Corinthians 8:4-6). The words 'by their nature' (physei) say that these beings are not gods in what they truly are. Paul is not saying the powers do not exist; he says they do not deserve to be served.

p: Paul corrects himself: what matters is not that we know God but that God knows us first.
b: 'To know' in the Bible is more than having facts. When God 'knows' someone he chooses and cares for that person (Amos 3:2; Jeremiah 1:5; Exodus 33:12). Paul turns the sentence around in mid-flight: the Galatians 'know God', but better, God knows them. That fits his whole argument: the believer's standing depends on what God has done, not on what the believer achieves. The passive 'to be known by God' appears again in 1 Corinthians 8:3 and 13:12. It prepares the next question: if God has taken hold of you, why go back and look for a status you already have?
orig: γνωσθέντες ὑπὸ θεοῦ (gnosthentes hypo theou), 'having been known by God'

t: How can Gentiles 'turn back' to the law?
p: The Galatians were never under the Torah, so how can taking it up be 'turning back'?
b: Paul has just said that Gentiles once served false gods (4:8). Now he says that taking up the law's calendar and circumcision is to turn back to 'those weak and poor elements' and be enslaved 'all over again'. But these Gentiles were never Jews. Three answers. (1) Paul puts the Torah, for Gentiles who adopt it as the way to belong, in the same class as their old religion, since both are 'elements' of the world before Christ. (2) The Galatian Gentiles once served the 'elements' as pagans, and any religion that depends on them is the same bondage, Jewish or not. (3) Paul is not condemning the Torah for Jews at all; he describes what it would become for Gentiles who took it up to gain a status Christ already gave them (a view of scholars who read Paul within Judaism). Jewish readers have often found the first answer deeply offensive; the third reading is one reason the New Perspective matters.

p: Is this the Jewish calendar, a pagan calendar, or both? Readers have answered all three ways.
b: Four terms of time: hemerai (days), menes (months), kairoi (seasons) and eniautoi (years). Most commentators hear the Jewish calendar: the Sabbath, the new moon, the festivals, and the Sabbath year (Leviticus 25; Colossians 2:16 lists festivals, new moons and Sabbaths together). Others hear the pagan calendar of astral and agricultural rites, since 4:3 and 4:9 speak of the 'elements', which include the sun, moon and stars. The verb paratereo means to observe closely, as Pharisees watched Jesus on the Sabbath (Luke 6:7). Paul does not tell Jews to stop keeping the Sabbath; he tells Gentiles that adding it to their faith as a requirement would undo what they received. Compare Romans 14:5: "One person judges one day to stand above another, and another judges every day alike." The churches have read this verse in different ways; see the card.
r: Colossians 2:16; Romans 14:5; Romans 14:6; Leviticus 23; Leviticus 25; Luke 6:7

a: be like me, for I have become like you
p: Paul asks them to become like him, because he became like them. Like him in what way?
b: The Greek has no verbs in the second half: 'as I, because I also as you'. Views: (1) Be free from the law as I am, since I gave up my Jewish way of life to live like a Gentile (1 Corinthians 9:21). (2) Be as I am in trusting Christ alone, since I stood where you stand, with no claim on God by birth or deeds (Philippians 3:7-9). (3) Imitate my steadiness: I did not give in to the demand for circumcision (2:3-5). Whatever the answer, Paul does not say he stopped being a Jew: the same letter calls him a Jew by birth (2:15), and Romans 11:1 and 2 Corinthians 11:22 say so plainly. Scholars of the 'Paul within Judaism' view press this point: Paul lives as a Jew who has joined Gentiles in Christ, and does not turn Gentiles into Jews.
r: 2:3; 2:4; 2:5; 2:15; Romans 11:1; 1 Corinthians 9:20; 1 Corinthians 9:21; 2 Corinthians 11:22; Philippians 3:5; Philippians 3:7

p: Something about Paul's body brought him to Galatia, and the Galatians did not turn away.
b: The Greek di' astheneian tes sarkos puts dia with the accusative, which normally means 'because of'. (The sense 'during' belongs to dia with the genitive.) So the plain reading is that the weakness was the occasion of Paul's first preaching to them: some illness brought him to the Galatians or kept him there. Nothing says what it was. Guesses: malaria, caught perhaps on a trip from the hot coast up to the high country of Pisidia; epilepsy (the spitting of 4:14 was a way people warded off it, and Lightfoot thought of it); an eye disease (4:15; 6:11); the 'thorn in the flesh' of 2 Corinthians 12:7; or the injuries from the stoning at Lystra (Acts 14:19). We do not know. 'The first time' (to proteron) can mean 'formerly' or 'the first of two visits'. That fits both the South Galatian view (Acts 13-14 and a return in Acts 14:21) and the North Galatian view (Acts 16:6 and 18:23), so it does not decide between them.
orig: δι᾽ ἀσθένειαν τῆς σαρκός (di' astheneian tes sarkos), 'because of a weakness of the flesh'

p: To spit was the ancient reflex against evil spirits, illness and bad luck.
b: The verb ekptyo is 'spit out'. People spat to ward off illness and bewitching. Pliny reports that people spat at epileptic fits and so 'threw back' the infection, and that they did the same against fascination (Natural History 28.35-36). Whether or not Paul's 'weakness' was epilepsy, the Galatians could have treated him as a person to be shunned, and Paul says they did the opposite. The word peirasmos ('test, trial') is the same one used of testing, and the Plain English Translation renders 'the test that my body brought you'. The Greek manuscripts differ on whether it was 'your test' or 'my test'; see the variant.

p: At Lystra the crowd called Paul and Barnabas Zeus and Hermes. Did the Galatians treat Paul like a messenger from heaven?
b: 'An angel' is a messenger, and in Greek religion a god's messenger was Hermes. The comparison with Christ Jesus himself is stronger. If the Galatian churches were those of Acts 13-14 (the South Galatian view), then Acts 14:11-13 gives a scene in the very region, where the people of Lystra took the visitors for gods. Ancient hospitality also held that gods might visit disguised as strangers (Acts 28:6; Hebrews 13:2). Paul's point has nothing to do with divinity, though: the Galatians welcomed him in his weakness as they would welcome God's own messenger, and now they treat him as a hostile stranger.

p: Was this a figure of speech for great sacrifice, or a hint that Paul's illness was in his eyes?
b: Two readings. (1) A proverb: giving one's eyes was a Greek way to say 'I would give my dearest possession'; commentators collect parallels. (2) A hint at disease: Paul's trouble was in his eyes, which some say would also explain why he writes in 'big letters' (6:11). Lightfoot examined this view at length and found that the arguments for it 'seem to melt away'. The text does not say. Either way the Galatians had once given Paul everything. The question 'Where is that joy?' (makarismos) can also be 'Where is your congratulating yourselves?', meaning the joy they felt at receiving the gospel.

a: just because I told you the truth
p: Ancient writers said a true friend speaks plainly and a flatterer smiles. Paul claims to be the friend.
b: Betz is among the scholars who read 4:12-20 beside ancient writing about friendship. Plutarch's essay How to Tell a Flatterer from a Friend is about this theme: the flatterer imitates the frank speech that belongs to the friend. So Paul's question is a rhetorical charge: those who now flatter you (4:17) are the false friends, and I am the true one. Notice that the rest of the letter has been blunt and sometimes harsh. This is the most personal section of the letter, though 6:1-2 and 6:18 are gentle too. The shift is on purpose, and Paul says so at 4:20.

p: 'To exclude you' leaves out the thing you would be shut out of. Readers fill it in four ways.
b: The Greek says only 'they want to exclude you' (ekkleisai). From what? (1) From Paul and his gospel, so the Galatians would depend on them. (2) From Christ and grace (5:4), so they would have to earn them (Lightfoot: 'shut you out from Christ'). (3) From the community of the covenant people: the Gentile believers will stay outside, as guests without full rights, until they are circumcised (a view held by many commentators). (4) From the local Jewish community, with which the Gentile believers had been closely linked (Nanos reads the agitators as local Jews, probably proselytes, who wanted the Gentile believers to become proselytes). Reading the opponents' views from Paul's replies ('mirror reading') is risky: Barclay has set out its limits. Everything we know about the agitators comes from Paul, who does not give them a hearing.

p: In one sentence Paul becomes a mother in labor and the Galatians the baby, and Christ the one being shaped.
b: Paul often uses family pictures for himself: a father (1 Corinthians 4:15), a nurse (1 Thessalonians 2:7). Here he says he is in labor, again, because their first birth in faith seems to have been lost. Gaventa calls this 'the maternity of Paul'. The second picture is odd: Christ is 'formed' (morphothe) in them, as if the believer were a womb or a statue in the making. The same family of words appears in Romans 8:29, where believers are "formed to match the image of his Son", and in 2 Corinthians 3:18. The point is that Christ's character is to take shape in a community, not that they need a rule.
orig: ὠδίνω ... μορφωθῇ (odino ... morphothe), 'I am in labor ... may be formed'

a: do you not hear what the law says?
p: Paul calls the book of Genesis 'the law' and says the Galatians have not truly heard it.
b: 'The law' (nomos) can mean one commandment, the whole Torah, or the whole Hebrew Scriptures. Here it is a story from Genesis. Jews called the five books of Moses the Torah, 'teaching', and the stories belong to it as much as the commands. 'Hear' reminds us that the Torah was heard in the synagogue, read aloud; the Galatians would have heard Genesis read. Paul's challenge is a bold one: the people who want to be 'under the law' (4:21) have not heard the law itself. Paul will argue from the Abraham story that belonging to Abraham comes by promise, which Genesis 15 gives before the command of circumcision in Genesis 17. A Jewish reader will note that Genesis 17 does command circumcision for Abraham's household; Paul's claim is about what that command was for, and he does not deny it for Jews.

p: Abraham had eight sons in all. Paul uses the two best known; Jewish tradition tidied the count.
b: Genesis names Ishmael (by Hagar, Genesis 16:15) and Isaac (by Sarah, Genesis 21:2-3), and later six sons by Keturah (Genesis 25:1-2). Some Jewish teachers identified Keturah with Hagar, so that Abraham's later wife was Hagar again (Genesis Rabbah 61:4, where Rav says Keturah is Hagar; the Targum of Jonathan on Genesis 25:1 says the same). Paul does not go there. He uses the two sons and two mothers of the main Genesis story. One view is that his readers knew it from synagogue hearing or from the agitators' own teaching; the letter does not say how Gentile Galatians would have learned it, so that is an assumption. For the story in its own setting see Genesis 16 and 21. For Hagar and Sarah as a pair, see the topic page.

p: Allegory, typology, midrash or a reply to opponents: what kind of reading is this?
b: The verb allegoreo occurs only here in the New Testament. It means 'to say one thing and mean another'. Greek teachers read Homer's gods as the forces of nature, and Philo of Alexandria read Genesis the same way: he made Sarah wisdom and Hagar the 'preliminary studies' that lead toward her (On Mating with the Preliminary Studies). Paul's use is different: he is reading history with the same shape as the present, which is usually called typology. Calvin objected, saying Paul's 'allegory' is a comparison, not a system of hidden meanings. The Plain English Translation keeps 'allegory' and lets the reader see the debate.

p: The pair is Sinai and the promise. Paul does not say 'old' and 'new' here.
b: In Galatians the first covenant is Sinai, with Hagar and slavery. The other is not named, but it is the promise to Abraham, given before Sinai and not cancelled by it (3:15-18). Paul in other letters contrasts the 'old' and 'new' covenants (2 Corinthians 3:6-14; Jeremiah 31:31-34), and later Christians often read this passage as 'Old Testament bad, New Testament good'. That reading is not in the text. Paul does not call the Sinai covenant false, since he writes, "The law, then, is holy. The commandment is also holy, and righteous, and good." (Romans 7:12), and he says of God, "For God does not take back his gifts and his call." (Romans 11:29). Messianic Jewish and 'Paul within Judaism' readers insist that the target is a way of using the law, not the Jewish people. See the card at 4:21-31.

p: Paul puts Mount Sinai in Arabia, where Hagar's descendants lived.
b: The Bible places Moses' meeting with God in Midian (Exodus 3:1), a land east of the Gulf of Aqaba, and in Paul's day 'Arabia' often meant the Nabataean kingdom, whose lands reached toward the Sinai region. Hagar's people, the Hagrites, lived in the same east (1 Chronicles 5:10, 19-20), and Ishmael's descendants lived in the desert (Genesis 25:18). So Hagar is tied to Arabia and Arabia to Sinai. Chrysostom already says that 'Hagar' is the word for Mount Sinai in the local language, and later writers took the Arabic word hajar, 'rock', as the link between Hagar and the mountain. Lightfoot discussed it at length and argued against it: he found the evidence that Arabs called Sinai by that name 'deficient in amount and suspicious in character', and doubted that Paul would have expected his Galatian readers to catch such a play on words. Paul went to Arabia himself soon after his call (1:17), and some think he went to Sinai like Elijah (1 Kings 19). Whatever the geography, the point is that Sinai lies outside the promised land, and Hagar the slave belongs there.

t: A word from the same root as 'elements'
p: The verb 'lines up with' comes from the same family as the 'elements' of 4:3 and 4:9.
b: Systoicheo means 'to stand in the same row or file'. Greek writers used it of soldiers in rank, and of a list of opposites in two columns: good and evil, light and dark, and so on. Paul sets out two columns: Hagar, Sinai, the present Jerusalem, slavery, the flesh; Sarah, the Jerusalem above, freedom, the promise, the Spirit. The verb shares its root with stoicheia (4:3, 9) and stoicheo (5:25), and some readers hear a deliberate echo. Some scholars build on this idea and read the 'elements' as the pairs in these columns. The Plain English Translation says 'lines up with' and keeps the root visible in notes.
orig: συστοιχεῖ (systoichei), 'stands in the same row with'

p: Who is 'the Jerusalem of today' and who are her slave children? The answer decides how the passage has been used.
b: Paul says the 'present Jerusalem' is in slavery with her children. Readings: (1) The actual city under Roman rule, a symbol of the age of the law (Lightfoot). (2) The Jerusalem church and its leaders, in so far as they favor the demand for circumcision (compare the men 'from James' at 2:12). (3) Judaism as a religion, which the church has too often taken Paul to mean, with terrible results in anti-Jewish teaching. Paul himself recognized the Jerusalem apostles as partners (2:9-10) and kept raising money for the poor there (Romans 15:25-27). Modern readers who place Paul within Judaism say the 'children' are those who want Gentiles to join the old order on those terms, not the Jewish people. Whatever the reading, Paul does not say 'the Jews'.

p: Jewish writers of Paul's time spoke of a heavenly Jerusalem that waits to come down.
b: The idea that the real Jerusalem and Temple exist in heaven, and will one day be revealed, was common in the Judaism of Paul's time. 2 Baruch 4:2-6 says God keeps the city in heaven, and 4 Ezra (chapters 9-10) sees a woman who turns into a city. Later Christian writers drew on it too (Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2). Paul adds 'mother', which fits Isaiah 54 (the next verse) and the Greek Old Testament's wording of Psalm 87:5, which calls Zion 'Mother Zion'. The reader should note that 'above' is not 'in the future' or 'in the next life'. It names a reality that already exists and already makes believers free.
r: 2 Baruch 4:2-6; 4 Ezra 10:25-54; Psalm 87:5; Hebrews 12:22; Revelation 21:2; Philippians 3:20

a: Be glad, barren woman, you who bear no children!
p: Paul quotes Isaiah's song to Zion after the exile and applies it to Sarah's side of the story.
b: Paul quotes the Septuagint of Isaiah 54:1. The Plain English Translation of the Hebrew reads: "Sing for joy, you barren one who has borne no child! Break out into a joyful song and shout, you who have not gone into labor!" (Isaiah 54:1). The Greek follows the Hebrew closely and Paul adds nothing. In Isaiah, the barren woman is Zion in exile, like Sarah (Isaiah 51:2-3) who also was barren and was given children; the 'married woman' is the Jerusalem that has husband and children, here taken as the Jerusalem of Paul's own day. By linking the verse with Sarah's story, Paul makes two points: the promise of children came to the barren one, and her children are more than the other's. The Gentiles, who are the 'many' here, were Isaiah's hope too (Isaiah 49:19-22; 54:3).

p: Isaac was born in the body of an old woman, yet Paul says he was born by the promise.
b: Isaac was also born in the flesh, to a woman who was past childbearing, so 'flesh' and 'promise' are not two kinds of birth in a biological sense. The contrast is in how: Ishmael came from the couple's plan (Genesis 16:2), Isaac came because God said "Sarah your wife will have a son" (Genesis 18:10). Paul says elsewhere that Abraham trusted the God "who makes the dead alive" (Romans 4:17), and that "the children born from the promise are the ones counted as his offspring" (Romans 9:8). The Gentile Galatians are children of the promise, as Isaac was, without circumcision and without being born into Israel by descent. A Jewish reader would stress what is not said: the promise to Israel is not cancelled (Romans 11:29).
r: Genesis 17:19; Genesis 18:10; Genesis 21:1; Romans 4:17; Romans 4:19; Romans 9:7; Romans 9:8

a: persecuted the child born by the Spirit
p: Genesis says Ishmael was 'laughing'. Jewish teachers read it as something worse, and Paul follows them.
b: Genesis 21:9 in the Plain English Translation reads: "Sarah saw that the son Hagar the Egyptian had borne to Abraham was laughing." The Hebrew verb metzachek is a pun on Isaac's name ('he laughs'). It could mean play, mock or worse. The Greek Old Testament adds 'with Isaac her son'. Rabbinic readings find a darker meaning. In Genesis Rabbah 53:11 Rabbi Akiva reads the word as sexual immorality, Rabbi Ishmael as idol worship, and Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei the Galilean as bloodshed; Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai gives a milder reading, that Ishmael was claiming the inheritance. Paul's 'persecuted' belongs to that stream of interpretation and does not come from the text of Genesis alone. He applies it to his own case: his own life is a record of persecution (5:11; 6:17), and the agitators are, on his reading, the descendants of the 'flesh' side.

a: Throw out the slave woman and her son.
p: Paul takes Sarah's harsh order and reads it as Scripture's verdict. The site's Genesis is close but not the same.
b: The Plain English Translation of Genesis reads: "Throw out this slave woman and her son. The son of this slave woman will not share the inheritance with my son, with Isaac." (Genesis 21:10). Paul drops 'this' and 'my son, with Isaac' and makes the sentence general. In Genesis, Abraham finds Sarah's demand terrible, and God tells him to listen to her (Genesis 21:11-12). Who is thrown out in Paul's story? Not Jews. Some scholars read it as an order to the Galatians to send away the agitators, which fits 5:12 (the Teachers, not the Jewish people). The command to 'throw out' has troubled many readers, and womanist readers (Delores Williams) say Paul's version erases Hagar's own story, in which God hears her and provides (Genesis 16:13; 21:17-19). Read slowly.

p: A yoke is a joy to some Jewish teachers and a weight to Paul. They speak of different people.
b: The yoke was a common picture of obligation. In Jewish writing 'the yoke of the Torah' and 'the yoke of the kingdom of heaven' were things to take up gladly (Mishnah Avot 3:5; Mishnah Berakhot 2:2). Jesus invites the weary to take his yoke: "Lift my yoke onto yourselves and learn from me, because I am gentle and my heart is humble." (Matthew 11:29). Paul calls the yoke 'of slavery' for Gentiles who think circumcision must be added to faith. At the Jerusalem meeting Peter spoke of "a yoke that neither our ancestors nor we ourselves had the strength to carry" (Acts 15:10). That is a Jewish believer speaking of what he would not put on Gentiles. Paul is not saying Jewish life under the Torah is a slave's life for Jews. He says it would be one for people who thought it earned them a place.
r: Matthew 11:29; Matthew 11:30; Acts 15:10; Mishnah Avot 3:5; Mishnah Berakhot 2:2

t: Why would Gentiles want to be circumcised?
p: For a Gentile man, circumcision was the door into Israel. Some teachers said it was needed.
b: Genesis 17 made circumcision the sign of the covenant for Abraham's household, and Jewish law required it of Gentile men who joined Israel as converts (proselytes). The question in the first century was whether Gentiles who honored Israel's God without converting, the 'God-fearers', also needed it. Josephus tells of King Izates of Adiabene (about AD 40s): one Jewish teacher, Ananias, told him he could worship God without circumcision, while another, Eleazar from Galilee, insisted that he must (Antiquities 20.34-48). Both views were held by Jews. On the usual reading the agitators in Galatia took Eleazar's side for Gentile Christ-followers; that is an inference, since the letter gives only Paul's side. Paul's reply is not that circumcision is bad for Jews, but that for Gentiles it would turn faith into a transaction. See the deep dive on this page.

a: bound to do the whole law
p: Paul warns that the man who takes on circumcision is taking on every command of the Torah.
b: A Gentile who became a proselyte accepted all of the commandments, and teachers were to tell him of the 'light' and 'heavy' ones (Babylonian Talmud Yevamot 47a-b, a later source describing the practice). So Paul's warning is a fair description of what conversion meant: the Galatians who were being urged to be circumcised may have been told it was a small step. Paul says it is the first step of a whole system. The point echoes Deuteronomy 27:26 and Galatians 3:10 (see there). James 2:10 makes a similar statement. Paul's 'whole law' differs from the 'whole law' of 5:14: here the sum of the commands to be done, there the law brought to its goal in love. The agitators themselves, Paul says in 6:13, do not keep the whole law.

p: In popular speech the phrase means a moral lapse. In Paul it means leaving a basis for a different one.
b: The Greek ex-epesate is 'you fell out of'. The Plain English Translation keeps 'fallen away'. 'Fallen from grace' now means a moral failure, as when a celebrity is disgraced. Paul means something else: moving from the ground of grace to the ground of law. The verb tenses show that he is describing people who are 'being justified' (present: trying to be) by law, and warns that this attempt cuts them off from Christ. Do these words describe true believers who lose salvation, or people who only appear to be believers, or a danger that has not yet happened? The churches disagree; see the card at this verse. Calvin held that 'falling from grace' means giving up the doctrine of grace and not losing the gift.
orig: τῆς χάριτος ἐξεπέσατε (tes charitos exepesate), 'you fell out of grace'

p: Is righteousness something believers already have, or something still hoped for at the last judgment?
b: Paul says believers wait with longing for 'the hope of righteousness'. The grammar allows several meanings. (1) The righteousness itself is hoped for: the final verdict of 'in the right' that God will speak on the last day. (2) The hope that comes from righteousness already given. (3) The hope that righteousness will one day become real in believers' lives . Some scholars argue that Paul sees justification in two stages: declared now by faith, confirmed on the day of judgment by the whole life the Spirit has produced (Romans 2:13; 8:33-34). Luther's tradition, for which justification is complete in Christ, reads the 'hope' as the assurance of what is already settled. The card at 2:16 in the earlier part sets out the churches' views of justification.

p: Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed readers all use this verse, and they hear it differently.
b: The Greek is pistis di' agapes energoumene. The participle can be middle ('working', 'being at work') or passive ('being put to work, made effective by love'). Either way love is the way faith shows itself. The Vulgate reads fides quae per caritatem operatur. Aquinas and the Council of Trent (session 6) understood faith as 'formed by love' (fides caritate formata): faith becomes a living, saving faith only when love shapes it. Luther rejected 'formed' faith: faith justifies alone, and love is its fruit. The Reformed (Calvin, the Westminster Confession) say the same: a living faith always produces love, though it justifies only because it holds on to Christ. In Paul's argument this is the replacement for circumcision: not a new work, but trust that acts in love (5:13-14).
orig: πίστις δι᾽ ἀγάπης ἐνεργουμένη (pistis di' agapes energoumene), 'faith working through love'

a: Who cut in front of you
p: Paul pictures the Galatians as runners who were doing well until someone cut in on them.
b: Paul often pictures his work as a race (2:2; 1 Corinthians 9:24; Philippians 2:16). The verb enkopto was used of cutting into a road to block it, or breaking a runner's stride. The question 'Who?' does not expect a name. It prepares the next verses, where the persuader is described without a name (5:8, 10). The fact that Paul does not name the troublemakers may mean the Galatians knew them well.

p: One proverb about yeast, used for harm here and for growth by Jesus in another place.
b: The saying is a proverb, and Paul quotes it again in 1 Corinthians 5:6. In Israel yeast was a picture of spread: it was banned in the Passover week because it worked through the dough (Exodus 12:15), and Jesus spoke of "the yeast of the Pharisees" (Mark 8:15). Later Jewish teachers used 'the yeast in the dough' for the evil impulse (Babylonian Talmud Berakhot 17a, a later source). What is the 'yeast' here? Views: the teaching of the agitators; the one troublemaker whose influence spreads (5:10); or the circumcision demand itself, which looks small but changes everything. In any case it supports 'do not give in even a little'.

a: the one who is disturbing you
p: Paul names no names. Scholars have identified the people who troubled Galatia in at least five ways.
b: Paul says 'the one who is disturbing you' (singular), and 'the people ... throwing you into turmoil' (5:12). Views, with their main supporters: (1) Jewish Christians from Judea or Jerusalem, who taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised (the traditional view). (2) Gentile believers in the Galatian churches who had become convinced it was needed (Munck, based on 6:13 if it says 'those who are circumcised'). (3) Local Jewish leaders who were not Christians and who pressed the Gentile Christ-followers to convert or leave (Nanos). (4) Judean Christians under Zealot pressure to avoid contact with the uncircumcised (Jewett). (5) Gnostics who asked for circumcision as a symbol, not as a work that earns merit (Schmithals; most scholars do not follow). All reconstruct from Paul's replies, which is why caution is needed. Nobody knows who the one in 5:10 is.

p: Someone said Paul still preached circumcision. Why would they say it, and what did he actually teach?
b: The charge may rest on what people knew of Paul. He had been a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5-6), and some scholars infer from that that he had once pressed the Torah on others, perhaps even on Gentiles, though the letter does not say so. And Paul had circumcised Timothy: "Paul wanted this man to set out with him. So he took Timothy and circumcised him, on account of the Jews living in that area, since everyone knew his father was Greek." (Acts 16:3). Or the claim may be that Paul preached circumcision to some audiences and not others. His own rule was: let each one stay as he was called (1 Corinthians 7:18-20). For Jews, circumcision stays; for Gentiles it is not asked. Scholars of the 'Paul within Judaism' view put it this way: Paul never told Jews to stop circumcising their sons. The point of 'still' is that Paul's opponents say he changed his message to please people (1:10).

t: The stumbling block of the cross
p: 'Skandalon' is a trap-stick. The cross trips up the hearer who wants a different Messiah.
b: Skandalon was the trigger of a trap, then anything that makes a person fall. Paul calls the crucified Messiah "a stumbling block to Jews" in 1 Corinthians 1:23. A Messiah executed as a cursed criminal ran against what many Jews expected, since Deuteronomy says "a man who is hanged is cursed by God" (Deuteronomy 21:23; see Galatians 3:13). For Gentiles it was foolish. Paul's argument here is simple: if he gave in on circumcision, the cross would stop being offensive, and the persecution would stop. It has not stopped, so he has not given in.

t: The sharpest sentence in the letter
p: Paul says he wishes the circumcision party would go all the way. Three layers of meaning.
b: The verb apokopto means 'cut off'. Readings: (1) A crude joke: if the knife is good for the foreskin, let it slip further. 'Mutilation' is Paul's sarcastic word for the circumcision party elsewhere (Philippians 3:2). (2) An echo of the pagan priests: the Galatians may have known of the eunuch priests (galli) of Cybele, the Mother of the Gods. Strabo (12.5.3) describes her great temple at Pessinus in Galatia and its priests, but does not mention castration there. The self-castration of Cybele's priests is told in Catullus 63, a poem built on the myth of Attis, and the link to Paul's words is a guess made by commentators. Circumcision would place them with those priests. (3) An echo of exclusion: "No man whose testicles are crushed or whose penis is cut off may enter the assembly of the LORD." (Deuteronomy 23:1). Paul wishes them cut off from the assembly. Modern readers find the line harsh. Jewish readers will remember that such sarcasm is aimed at the agitators, and does not say anything about Jewish circumcision itself.

t: Flesh: body, family, or a power?
p: Paul's word 'flesh' has three meanings in one letter. The Plain English Translation keeps one English word.
b: Sarx is the soft part of a body. In Galatians it is (1) the physical body (4:13, 'weakness of the flesh'; 2:20); (2) the human, physical way of doing things, as in 4:23, 29 and the ordinary birth of Ishmael; and (3) from here on, a force that pulls the self against the Spirit (5:16-17, 19, 24; 6:8). The Plain English Translation keeps 'flesh' every time, as the site's term list requires, and does not use 'sinful nature' (a modern choice that hides the connection with circumcision, the cutting of the flesh, in 6:12-13). Paul does not despise the body: the flesh is a power that is crucified (5:24), not a shell to discard. Romans 7-8 uses the word in the same way.

p: Freedom, for Paul, ends in service. The same word that described the old bondage now describes love.
b: The verb is douleuo, 'be a slave'. It is the verb of bondage in 4:8-9, 25, and now Paul applies it to love: "Through love, be slaves to one another." This is a deliberate paradox. Believers were set free from slavery to the elements and the law (4:1-9), and are then to bind themselves to each other. The agitators offer a slavery to rules, Paul offers slavery to the neighbor. The difference is that the slavery of love is free (5:13) and fulfills the law (5:14). Jewish readers might also compare the Hebrew 'ebed, the servant of God who is honored. See the topic on freedom.

a: You are to love your neighbor as yourself
p: Paul quotes the line that Jewish teachers and Jesus called the center of the law.
b: The Plain English Translation of Leviticus reads: "Do not take vengeance, and do not keep a grudge against the children of your people. You are to love your neighbor as yourself. I am the LORD." (Leviticus 19:18). Paul's Greek follows the Septuagint. Rabbi Akiva called this line 'the central tenet of the Torah' (Genesis Rabbah 24:7), and Hillel told a would-be convert that the rest is commentary on 'what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor' (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 31a, a later source). Jesus joined it to the Shema: "The whole law hangs from these two commandments, and the Prophets too." (Matthew 22:40). Romans 13:8 says "Whoever loves the other person has fulfilled the law." Paul and the Jewish teachers agree on the line; the difference is what they say Gentiles must do about the rest of the Torah.
r: Leviticus 19:18; Matthew 22:39; Matthew 22:40; Mark 12:31; Romans 13:8; Romans 13:10; James 2:8

p: 'Walk' is the Bible's word for a way of life, and the Hebrew word for Jewish law is built on it.
b: To 'walk' (peripateo) is to live. The Hebrew root halak, 'walk', gave the name of the legal side of Judaism, halakhah, 'the way of walking'. Psalm 1:1 and Psalm 119:1 speak of walking in the Lord's way, and the Qumran Community Rule says that people 'walk' in the ways of the two spirits. When Paul tells the Galatians to 'walk by the Spirit' he is giving them a halakhah of their own, a way of life for Gentile followers of the Messiah that does not run through the Torah's commands for Israel. Romans 8:4 uses the same verb (peripateo).
orig: πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε (pneumati peripateite), 'walk by the Spirit'
r: 5:25; Psalm 1:1; Psalm 119:1; Romans 8:4; Romans 13:13; Community Rule 3-4

a: so that you do not do whatever you wish
t: Who is stopped from doing what?
p: The purpose clause can mean the Spirit blocks your bad wishes, or the flesh blocks your good ones.
b: 'So that you do not do whatever you wish' has two main readings. (1) The flesh and the Spirit hold each other in check, so that a believer cannot simply follow either one on impulse; the Spirit blocks the flesh's wishes (Burton). (2) The flesh stands in the way of the good the believer wants to do (Luther and Calvin: the believer's lifelong struggle, as in Romans 7:15-20). A third reading takes it as describing the state before the Spirit rules, so that it does not describe the mature believer (held by some interpreters; no teacher is named here). The Methodist card gives Wesley's own words. Compare Romans 7:15: the divided 'I' is a frequent link. Paul's purpose here is practical: Galatians who are led by the Spirit do not need the law's fence (5:18), and those who are not led do not get a safe place from the flesh by keeping the law (5:19-21).

t: Led by the Spirit, not under law
p: Does 'not under law' set Jewish believers free from the Torah, or only Gentiles from a burden they never had?
b: Compare Romans 8:14: "As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are God's children." 'Under law' has a set meaning in Galatians: it is the condition of those held in custody until Christ came (3:23; 4:4-5). Views: it is true of every believer, Jew and Gentile (a traditional Protestant view); it is true of Gentile believers, who never were under the Torah's covenant and are told they should not put themselves there (a view of scholars who read Paul within Judaism); it describes the way the law works as a controlling power, which does not decide whether a Jewish Christian should continue to keep the Torah as a way of life. Acts shows Paul keeping Jewish practices (Acts 21:23-26), and 1 Corinthians 9:20 says he lived as 'under law' with Jews 'though not myself under law'. The verse sits between two uses of 'law' (5:14, 23), which is why it needs care.

p: Greek moralists and Jewish teachers both wrote lists of vices. Paul's is aimed at the Galatian church's own life.
b: Lists of vices were common in Greek philosophy and Hellenistic Judaism (Wisdom of Solomon 14:25-26; Philo). The Community Rule from Qumran has a list of the 'spirit of falsehood' set against a list for the 'spirit of truth'. Paul's list has four groups: sexual sin (immorality, uncleanness, shameless living), false worship (idol worship, sorcery), social breakdown (hatreds, fighting, jealousy, anger, selfish ambition, splits, factions, envy), and excess (drunkenness, wild parties). The social items are the longest, and they are the very things Paul sees in Galatia (5:15, 26). The list is not complete, as 'things like these' shows. Compare Romans 1:29-31 and 1 Corinthians 6:9-10. The Greek word for 'sexual immorality' is porneia; see the topic.
r: 5:15; 5:26; Romans 1:29; Romans 13:13; 1 Corinthians 6:9; 1 Corinthians 6:10; Community Rule 4:2-11; Wisdom of Solomon 14:25

p: The Greek word 'hairesis' means a choice or a party. It became the church's word for heresy.
b: Hairesis meant 'choice', then a school or party within Judaism: Acts calls the Pharisees and Sadducees a hairesis (Acts 5:17; 15:5; 26:5), and the Jewish leaders called Paul's followers the hairesis of the Nazarenes (Acts 24:5). In 1 Corinthians 11:19 it is divisions inside a church, and here it is another word for the splits Paul fears in Galatia. The sense of a wrong teaching is found by the late first or early second century (2 Peter 2:1 speaks of haireseis of destruction, and Titus 3:10 of a hairetikos), and scholars disagree on how early. In Galatians it most likely still means a party or faction. The Plain English Translation says 'factions'.
r: Acts 5:17; Acts 15:5; Acts 24:5; Acts 26:5; 1 Corinthians 11:19; 2 Peter 2:1

p: Paul warns that those who 'practice' these things will not inherit God's kingdom. To whom is the warning given?
b: The verb is present: people who keep on doing such things, as a way of life. The warning is addressed to the church ('I told you before'). Views: it is a real danger for believers, who can lose their inheritance by persistent sin (Catholic teaching on mortal sin, Orthodox, Wesleyan); it describes people who show by their life that they never truly had faith (Reformed); or it is a general statement of the two ways that leaves open how the Spirit protects those who are truly his. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 and Ephesians 5:5 say much the same, and 6:7-8 of this letter warns that sowing to the flesh ends in decay. The card on 5:4 sets out the churches' views.

p: 'Works of the flesh' are plural and made. 'Fruit of the Spirit' is singular and grows.
b: Paul does not say 'works of the Spirit'. The flesh produces erga, deeds, many and scattered; the Spirit yields karpos, fruit, one, grown and not made. That choice avoids the language of 'works of the law' (2:16; 3:2), and it says that the life of love comes by the Spirit's power, not by a list of rules. The nine terms are often grouped in threes. Jewish and Greek lists of virtue existed (Qumran Community Rule 4:2-6 lists the truth spirit's fruits; Greek moral writers list cardinal virtues), but the list here has love first and is built on the Spirit. The topic page gathers the passage.

p: The same Greek word that Paul uses for 'faith' appears in the list. Here the Plain English Translation says 'faithfulness'.
b: Pistis is 'faith' almost everywhere in Galatians. In a list of habits of character, most translators take it as 'faithfulness' or 'reliability' (the KJV has 'faith'). The context points that way: the other items are traits that show in dealings with others. Some see a connection with Paul's other uses: the person who trusts is the person who can be trusted, and faith is born from the Spirit (3:2, 5). A small number of readers keep 'faith'. The site's term for pistis is 'faith' by default and 'trust' by context; here the context calls for a quality of character.

a: No law stands against things like these.
p: Aristotle used almost the same words for a person so good that law cannot touch him.
b: Aristotle wrote that for the person who is better than all the rest "there is no law" over such people, 'for they are themselves law' (Politics 3.13). Paul's phrase has the same form (kata ton toiouton ouk estin nomos). Paul's point may use the same understatement: the Spirit's people do not need a legal fence. The words also work against the agitators, who want law imposed on people whom the Spirit already leads. Yet the line cannot mean that Paul rejects all law: in the next chapter he speaks of "the law of Christ" (6:2).

a: fall in line with the Spirit
p: The verb Paul uses for living by the Spirit is related to the 'elements' he rejected.
b: Stoicheo means 'to stand in line, to march in step', and it is related to stoicheia, the 'elements' of 4:3 and 4:9, and to systoicheo in 4:25. For Paul, the Galatians must either line up behind the elements (and the present Jerusalem) or fall in line with the Spirit. The verb is used again in Romans 4:12, "walk in the steps of that faith", and in Philippians 3:16. A related 5:16 verb, peripateo 'walk', is about everyday life; this one is more military: keep rank. The Plain English Translation says 'fall in line' to keep the word-family visible.

a: put that person back on his feet
p: The verb is the one for mending a net or setting a bone. The aim is repair.
b: Katartizo means to put in order, to mend: the fishermen 'mend' their nets (Mark 1:19), and a doctor 'sets' a bone. 'Overtaken' (prolemphthe) can mean surprised by sin, or caught in the act. Paul does not say who is to do it, only 'you who live by the Spirit'. That may mean the mature, or (given 5:25) all who are led by the Spirit, and not a special class. The method, 'a gentle spirit', is the Spirit's fruit (5:23) and the warning, 'look to yourself', is to avoid pride. Compare Matthew 18:15, "If he listens to you, you have won your brother back." Later church discipline often has less gentleness than Paul asks for.

p: Five readings of a phrase Paul uses only here (compare 1 Corinthians 9:21).
b: After a letter that warns against 'law', Paul speaks of a 'law of Christ'. (1) The Torah as Christ interprets and fulfills it, a kind of new Torah (compare Matthew 5:17-20). (2) The command of love, which sums up the law (5:14; Romans 13:10, "love is the law fulfilled") (some scholars). (3) The pattern of Christ's own self-giving, which believers re-enact by carrying each other (Hays). (4) Christ's whole teaching, the sayings and example he gave. (5) The law of Moses itself, now written on hearts by the Spirit and kept in love (compare Romans 8:4). The Plain English Translation says 'the law of Christ' without choosing. The verb 'fulfill' ties it to 5:14.
r: 5:14; 5:23; 1 Corinthians 9:21; Romans 8:2; Romans 13:8; Romans 13:10; Matthew 5:17; James 1:25

p: Paul uses two different words for load in three verses. The Plain English Translation tries to show it.
b: Verse 2 uses bare, 'weights, crushing loads', which two people can share. Verse 5 uses phortion, a pack or cargo: the soldier's kit, the traveler's baggage, a load each one is given. The two verses do not contradict. Overwhelming troubles are to be carried together; the daily pack of each person's own task and account before God is one's own. Compare Romans 14:12 for the 'account' idea. Matthew 11:30 uses phortion too: "the load I give is light." (Matthew 11:30).

p: 'Each will carry his own load' sounds like it cancels 6:2. It does not.
b: The future 'will carry' may point to the day when each gives an account (Romans 14:12; 2 Corinthians 5:10). Or it may be a present truth: each person has a personal share of work and responsibility that no one else can do. The verses on each side, 6:4 about testing one's own work, and 6:3 on thinking too much of oneself, support this reading. See the note on 6:2 for the two Greek words.

a: the one who is being taught the word
p: The Greek verb behind 'taught' is where the word 'catechism' comes from.
b: Both 'taught' and 'teaches' are forms of katecheo, 'to sound down into the ear', to instruct by voice. It is a rare word in the New Testament (Luke 1:4; Acts 18:25; 1 Corinthians 14:19), and here Paul uses it for a regular arrangement: churches had teachers, and teachers were supported by the students. Paul himself usually refused pay (1 Corinthians 9:12-18), but he defends the right to it (1 Corinthians 9:14), as the Didache does later (chapter 13). 'Partner' (koinoneo) is the word for sharing property or money. The command comes in the middle of a call to carry each other's loads.
orig: κατηχούμενος ... κατηχοῦντι (katechoumenos ... katechounti), 'the one taught ... the one teaching'

a: Whatever a person sows, that is what he will also reap
p: A proverb found across the Bible. Paul uses it for both generosity and the contest between flesh and Spirit.
b: Sowing and reaping were Israel's picture of cause and effect. Job's friend says "whoever plows wickedness and plants misery gets a harvest of it" (Job 4:8), and Proverbs says "Plant wrongdoing and you will harvest disaster" (Proverbs 22:8). Hosea has the good side: "Sow for yourselves in righteousness; reap by the measure of loyal love." (Hosea 10:12). In 2 Corinthians 9:6 Paul uses the image for giving money. That makes some scholars think 6:7 grows out of 6:6 (support your teachers). The verb 'sneered at' (mykterizo) means 'turn up the nose at'. The warning is that God cannot be tricked by a show of faith.

p: Do good to all, but start at home. Paul gives the church a family's duties to each other.
b: The Greek oikeios means 'belonging to the household'. Paul's rule has two parts: good to everyone, with priority to fellow believers. The order is realistic, not selfish; a small, poor church can only do so much (compare 1 Timothy 5:8; Ephesians 2:19). It may echo the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, which Paul agreed to at the meeting (2:10); the text does not say so. The word 'faith' here may mean the Christian faith (the trust, the community) as in 1:23 and 3:23. In Greek thought, being related by household made help a duty, so Paul is naming the church as a family.
orig: οἰκείους τῆς πίστεως (oikeious tes pisteos), 'members of the household of the faith'

p: Up to here a scribe wrote; now Paul takes the pen. His 'big letters' have raised three explanations.
b: Paul usually dictated and then signed (Romans 16:22 names the scribe Tertius; 1 Corinthians 16:21; Colossians 4:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17). The Greek 'I have written' is the way of speaking in a letter: it means 'I am writing'. Why the large letters? (1) For emphasis, as in a poster. (2) The handwriting of a person who is not a trained scribe. (3) Poor eyesight, which some say fits 4:13-15; Lightfoot rejected that account and thought the large letters were better explained another way. Whichever it is, the final lines (6:11-18) are a signed summary of the whole letter, and in ancient practice a signature could give a letter its authority.

a: make a fine appearance in the flesh
p: Paul says the agitators have their own interest. Scholars suggest what the pressure was.
b: The word euprosopeo occurs only here: 'to make a good face'. Paul says they want to look good, and to escape persecution 'because of the cross'. Views: Jewish believers in Judea were pressed by Zealot groups to avoid easy contact with the uncircumcised, and the agitators needed Gentile converts to be circumcised to protect themselves (Jewett). Or, if the agitators were Jewish leaders in Galatia, they wanted the Gentile believers seen as proper converts and not as a rival group (Nanos). Both agree that Paul reads the motive as fear, not conviction.

a: do not keep the law, either
t: 'They do not keep the law themselves'
p: Paul says the circumcision party does not keep the law. What does he mean?
b: The Greek manuscripts disagree on 'those who are getting circumcised' or 'those who have been circumcised' (see the variant). Views: (1) Paul charges hypocrisy: those who urge the whole law do not themselves do all of it. (2) Paul makes a point he has made already: no one keeps the whole law, so no one can be justified by it (3:10-12; Romans 2:17-24; 3:9-20). (3) The agitators are Gentile converts who were circumcised and only picked parts of the law (Munck). A Jewish reader will note the charge is aimed at these people, not at Jews generally. The aim, Paul says, is to 'boast about your flesh', to count the Gentiles circumcised as a success for their own group.

a: boast in anything but the cross
p: A Roman would have thought a cross was the last thing to boast about.
b: Crucifixion was a punishment of the Roman state for slaves and rebels. Cicero said the very word 'cross' should be far from the thoughts of a Roman citizen (For Rabirius 16). Studies of crucifixion show how shameful it was. Paul boasts of it, and in doing so he applies the call to boast only in the LORD to the cross: "If anyone is to boast, let it be in this alone: that he shows insight and knows me, that I am the LORD" (Jeremiah 9:24). Paul uses the same idea, 'boast in the Lord', in 1 Corinthians 1:31. The world is 'crucified to me', and I to the world: the 'world' (kosmos) of elements, flesh and religion-as-status is finished. This gathers 2:19-20; 4:3; 5:24; 6:15. The Plain English Translation says 'through which' because the nearest noun is 'the cross'. The Greek di' hou could also be 'through whom', that is, through the Lord Jesus Christ, and commentators divide; the sense is much the same.

a: A new creation is what matters
p: Circumcision and uncircumcision are both nothing. A Jewish apocalyptic hope takes their place.
b: The hope for a new creation is in Isaiah: "For look, I am creating new heavens and a new earth." (Isaiah 65:17). Jewish writings of Paul's time spoke of a renewed creation at the end (Jubilees 1:29; 4:26; 1 Enoch 72:1). Paul says it has begun in Christ (2 Corinthians 5:17). Later rabbinic sources said a convert to Judaism is like a newborn child (Babylonian Talmud Yevamot 22a, 48b), and Paul may be answering that idea. A Gentile who believes is already a new creation and needs no second birth by conversion. The verse repeats 5:6 and 3:28.

p: A canon was a measuring rod. Paul's 'rule' is the line he has just drawn.
b: Kanon is a straight rod for measuring (2 Corinthians 10:13-16 uses it for a field of work). Later 'canon' was the church's word for its list of Scriptures and rule of faith, but that is not what Paul means. The 'rule' is the saying just before it: a new creation, not circumcision or uncircumcision (6:15), or perhaps the cross (6:14). 'Walk' is the verb of 5:16.

p: 'Peace and mercy upon Israel' sounds like a Jewish blessing.
b: The Psalms end with 'Peace on Israel' (Psalm 125:5; 128:6), and the Jewish Eighteen Benedictions (the daily prayer) ask for peace and mercy on Israel (commentators compare the blessing for peace, but the wording differs between versions, and its date is later). Paul's use, 'peace and mercy', shows him writing as a Jew at the end of a letter that has sharp words for Gentile Christians who want to be Jews. The next phrase, 'the Israel of God', ends the letter on the same note.

p: The only place Paul uses these words. Is it the church, Jewish believers, or the Jewish people?
b: Paul uses these exact words only here. Readings: (1) The church of Jews and Gentiles together, with kai ('and') meaning 'even' (Calvin: all believers, 'whether Jews or Gentiles'; Lightfoot: the 'spiritual Israel generally'). (2) Jews, in particular the pious remnant of Israel, set beside the 'all who walk by this rule' (Burton). (3) The Jewish people as a whole, for whom Paul asks mercy, as in Romans 11:26. Chrysostom takes the phrase to mean those who keep this rule and 'follow after grace'. The grammar of kai allows 'and also' or 'even'. Burton argued against 'even' because the order 'peace and mercy' reads oddly if both belong to one group, and because he found no place where Paul uses 'Israel' for anyone but the Jewish nation or part of it. The word order does not settle the matter. The question bears on whether the church replaces Israel, which Paul denies in Romans 11:1. See the card.

p: The Greek word 'stigma' meant a brand. Paul's body carried the scars of his work.
b: Stigmata were brands or tattoos: a slave's owner's mark, the sign of a soldier, a god's devotee. Views: (1) scars from beatings and stoning (2 Corinthians 11:23-25; Acts 14:19, "pelted Paul with stones and hauled him outside the town"; Acts 16:22-23). (2) A slave's brand: Paul as Christ's slave (1:10; Romans 1:1). (3) A sacred mark that protects, as some religious people carried the name of their god, so that no one dare 'cause me trouble'. From the thirteenth century the word was used for the wounds of Jesus said to appear on saints, beginning with Francis of Assisi in 1224. Catholic teaching does not require belief in any particular case, and Protestant interpreters do not read Galatians 6:17 that way.

p: Paul's last word before 'Amen' in Greek is 'brothers'. After a sharp letter, the ending is affectionate.
b: In Greek, the last word before 'Amen' is 'brothers'. Other letters of Paul close with 'grace be with you', and this one adds the address. The letter has no thanksgiving at its start and no list of personal greetings at its end, which is unlike most of Paul's letters. The grace that opened the letter (1:3) closes it. Many manuscripts add a note that the letter was written from Rome; it is a later addition (see the variant).
